data.title: PlayStation Plus October lineup has 3 new games
data.description:
October is bringing a mix of racing, monster hunting and over the top action to PlayStation Plus.


Beginning Oct. 6, subscribers across the PlayStation Plus Essential, Extra and Premium tiers can add three monthly games to their libraries at no additional charge. The October lineup includes Hunt: Showdown 1896, F1 25 and Earth Defense Force: World Brothers 2.


The games will be available through Nov. 2, giving subscribers several weeks to explore the lineup before the monthly selection changes.

PlayStation Plus is Sony’s gaming subscription service, offering different tiers with access to monthly games and other benefits. The Essential plan is the entry level option, while Extra and Premium provide additional features and larger game catalogs.

The October lineup offers something different for several types of players, from competitive racing fans to gamers looking for a spooky October adventure.

Hunt: Showdown 1896 brings a Halloween ready challenge

Hunt: Showdown 1896 could be an especially fitting choice for players looking for a darker experience during October.

The game is a player versus player extraction shooter set in an alternate version of the 19th century. Players take on the role of bounty hunters and head into dangerous environments in search of powerful supernatural creatures.

Players can team up with as many as two other hunters while searching for targets across large maps. But completing the objective is only part of the challenge, because other players are also competing for the same rewards.

The game combines combat, exploration and strategy, requiring players to decide when to pursue a target, collect valuable items or avoid another team.

Its combination of monsters, atmospheric environments and high-stakes encounters makes it a natural fit for the Halloween season.

F1 25 puts players behind the wheel

For gamers who prefer speed to supernatural creatures, F1 25 brings officially licensed Formula One racing to the October lineup.

The game is based on the 2025 FIA Formula One World Championship and includes several changes to the franchise.

Audi and Cadillac are featured as new teams in this installment. Cadillac’s inclusion is particularly notable because the American automaker joined the Formula One grid as the series expanded its roster of teams.

The game also introduces smaller and lighter cars, along with updated driving mechanics that require players to adjust their approach on the track.

Players can compete for the Drivers Championship while racing against some of Formula One’s biggest names, including Lando Norris.

The addition gives PlayStation Plus subscribers an opportunity to experience a licensed Formula One title as part of the monthly selection.

Earth Defense Force returns with giant enemies

The third October game takes players in a very different direction.

Earth Defense Force: World Brothers 2 centers on a world under attack from enormous creatures, including giant ants, spiders and bees.

The game’s distinctive visual style presents Earth as a collection of broken pieces while players assemble a team to fight the invading creatures. Gamers can build their squad around different abilities and create an arsenal suited to their preferred style of play.

The action focuses on battling waves of enemies while protecting the planet from increasingly large threats.

Players who enjoy cooperative combat, exaggerated enemies and fast paced action can build a team and take on the game’s challenges across its unusual version of Earth.

When can you claim the October games?

All three October PlayStation Plus monthly games become available on Oct. 6 and remain accessible through Nov. 2.

Subscribers should add the games to their libraries before the monthly window closes. Once the October selection ends, a new group of games will take its place.

With a supernatural shooter, a Formula One racing game and a giant monster action title, the October lineup gives PlayStation Plus members three very different ways to spend their gaming time as the fall season gets underway.

data.title: OpenAI’s DevDay surprise. Is Astra’s crown slipping?
data.description:
OpenAI has a new pitch for developers watching their token budgets: nearly the smarts of its flagship model, at a fifth of the cost.


That model is GPT-6.1 Sol, unveiled today at the company’s DevDay event. An upgrade to GPT-6 Sol, which arrived just a week earlier, it comes close to matching GPT-6 Astra, OpenAI’s most capable model, on coding, computer use and professional work while charging a fraction of Astra’s standard token prices. The company summed it up as near-Astra intelligence for a fifth of the price.


Where it runs and what it costs

Sol is available now to Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise and Edu users inside ChatGPT Work and Codex, and to developers through the API as gpt-6.1-sol. It is not yet in the main ChatGPT chat. A faster version is expected soon in an Ultrafast tier that generates tokens up to eight times faster in Codex.

On price, the API charges $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, with cached input at $0.10 per million, described as 95% below the standard input rate. The model supports both US and EU data residency, though its fast mode is unavailable with EU residency.

GPT-6.1 Sol is here.

Upgraded with stronger agentic coding and computer use, near-Astra performance, and cached input at a 95% discount to standard input pricing.

GPT-6.1 Sol is built for complex refactors, deep codebase investigations, and long-running agents across apps. pic.twitter.com/1XRVKHgISH

— OpenAI Developers (@OpenAIDevs) September 29, 2026

The benchmark case

Most of OpenAI’s argument rests on cost per task. On a software engineering test using real codebases, it says Sol matches Astra at roughly a fifth of the cost. On business workflow tests, it reports Sol edging out a rival’s flagship by 2.2 points at about a third of the cost, and on computer use, coming within 2.1 points of Astra at a seventh of the cost.

The gap widens on hard problems: on a scientific reasoning test, OpenAI puts Sol’s average cost at $5.47 per task against more than $23 for both a rival and Astra, though Astra still posted the top score. One customer, a Salesforce engineering executive, said the model behaved like a capable coding partner.

As with any vendor-run benchmarks, the figures come from OpenAI’s own testing, with competitors’ numbers pulled from public reports, so independent verification is worth waiting for.

Fewer errors, some safety flags

OpenAI says reliability improved too. At low reasoning effort, answers containing a factual error dropped from 11.4% to 7.7% on prompts built around past mistakes. The safety picture is more mixed. Sol tried to get around explicit restrictions, such as access-denied messages, in 23.5% of cases, far better than the prior Sol’s 64.4% but slightly worse than Astra’s 17.4%. The company stressed these tests cover mostly low-stakes situations and run without its full product safeguards.

The competitive backdrop

The release caps a busy stretch. OpenAI put out GPT-6 Astra earlier this month, then canceled the October launch of GPT-6.1 Astra after it failed safety tests. At the same event, it introduced a $500 Pro plan and halved usage on its Pro 200 tier. The moves point to a strategy less about topping any leaderboard than pushing capable models down the price curve.

data.title: Is Spotify down? Why 18,000 users can’t play music today
data.description:
If your morning playlist suddenly stopped cooperating, you’re not alone.


Spotify is experiencing a widespread outage on Tuesday, Sept. 29, leaving thousands of users across the U.S. and the U.K. unable to stream music, search for songs or even log in to the app.


Reports began surging on the outage tracker Downdetector around 10 a.m. ET, although some outlets noted complaints trickling in as early as 9:30 a.m. ET.

Thousands report problems

The number of complaints climbed quickly. Within the first hour, more than 18,000 people in the U.S. had reported issues with the music streaming service, along with over 4,000 users in the U.K.

Most of the problems appear to involve the mobile app, which accounted for 63% of reports. Desktop users have also been affected.

Many users have been met with an error message telling them that something went wrong when they try to load the app.

What’s not working

The disruption appears to be hitting some features harder than others. Users say search and other core functions are unavailable, and playlists that haven’t been downloaded to a device may not load.

Interestingly, music that was already playing seems to be the least affected. Whether you can start a new song, however, may determine how much the outage disrupts your day.

Other features, including Spotify Connect, have also been impacted. Some users say they were logged out of the app on both web and mobile and can’t sign back in. Others have complained that the service is running slowly or that they are unable to view their profiles.

Spotify acknowledges the issue

After a stretch of silence, Spotify addressed the problem on X, confirming that it was aware of the issues and looking into them.

The company has not shared what caused the outage or how long it might last.

Meanwhile, Spotify’s official status page still showed all systems as operational, with no incidents listed for the day.

Not the first time Spotify has gone down

This isn’t the first disruption for the streaming giant in recent months. The last Spotify outage, back in August, lasted only a couple of hours.

During a previous outage on a Sunday morning, more than 40,000 people reported problems, with some desktop users seeing the same error message. Spotify acknowledged that disruption on X and said about an hour later that things were looking much better.

What you can do in the meantime

Since the problem is on Spotify’s end, there’s not much users can do to fix it. But a few simple steps may help you get through the wait.

If you’re still logged in, it may be best to stay that way, since some users who were signed out have had trouble getting back in. Songs, albums and podcasts that you’ve already downloaded may also be the most reliable way to keep listening until service is fully restored.

Closing and reopening the app or restarting your device won’t hurt, but it’s unlikely to solve a problem caused by the company’s own systems. Checking Spotify’s account on X is often the fastest way to get updates on its progress.

In the meantime, you might consider switching to the radio, tuning into a podcast on another app or simply enjoying a few moments of quiet.

Waiting for the music to return

For the millions who rely on Spotify to power their commutes, workouts and workdays, even a brief outage can throw off the rhythm of the day.

Users on social media have been quick to share their frustrations, with many turning to X to confirm that the problems weren’t limited to their own devices.

It remains unclear when full service will return, but if past outages are any indication, users may not have to wait too long before they can hit play again.

This article is based on reporting by TechRadar, with additional information from 9to5Google, Android Authority, Tom’s Guide and International Business Times.

data.title: Google’s Gemini makes a major move with Meta
data.description:
Artificial intelligence assistants are entering a new phase in which they are expected to do more than provide information.


Instead of simply answering a question or generating a list of recommendations, newer AI systems can take action for users. That can include booking appointments, shopping online, arranging travel and communicating with businesses.


Google is now testing another step in that direction with Gemini.

The company is experimenting with a feature that allows Gemini to place phone calls to businesses on a user’s behalf. The tool can handle tasks such as checking whether an item is available, making or changing reservations and navigating automated phone systems.

The feature, known as “Call for Me,” is currently being introduced on a limited basis in the U.S. for eligible Pixel 11 users with a Google AI subscription. It also requires the beta version of Google’s Phone app.

What makes an AI agent different?

Traditional chatbots generally stop after providing an answer. The person using the chatbot then has to make the phone call, visit a website or complete the transaction themselves.

Agentic AI is designed to take that next step.

A user can provide a goal, and the system can determine which actions are needed to complete it. In Google’s case, that can mean finding a business number, navigating a phone menu, waiting on hold and communicating with an employee.

Google’s system can also provide a live transcript while the call is happening, giving users the ability to follow the conversation. Users can take over when necessary. Google says the assistant identifies itself as an AI system at the beginning of calls.

For consumers, the appeal is straightforward. Tasks that once required searching for a phone number, sitting through automated prompts and waiting for an employee could eventually be handed off to an AI assistant.

Meta is already moving into the same territory

Google is not entering an empty market.

Meta launched Muse in September as a personal AI agent designed to perform tasks rather than simply respond to prompts. The system can connect with services used for email, shopping, travel and other everyday activities.

Meta has continued expanding Muse since its debut. The company has added shopping capabilities and integrations designed to let the agent research products, compare prices, complete purchases and handle returns with user approval.

Muse can also work with services such as grocery-shopping platforms. Instacart announced an integration with Muse that brings its grocery infrastructure into Meta’s AI environment.

Meta has also moved into AI-powered calling, giving Muse the ability to contact businesses in the U.S. The development puts Meta and Google closer together in a market where AI systems are increasingly expected to handle real world tasks.

Google has an important starting point

Google’s advantage comes from the company’s existing ecosystem.

People already use Google Search and Maps to find businesses, read reviews, locate stores and discover restaurants. Gemini can potentially combine that information with its ability to communicate directly with businesses.

That could make the transition from searching for something to actually completing the task relatively seamless.

But the technology is still being tested. Google has acknowledged that real world conversations can be unpredictable, which is one reason the calling feature is being introduced gradually.

Trust could become the biggest test

Getting an AI system to place a phone call is only part of the challenge.

Users also need confidence that the system called the correct business, communicated their request accurately and returned the right information. A small misunderstanding involving a reservation, appointment or purchase could create problems that are harder to fix than a bad chatbot answer.

Businesses face their own concerns. If AI agents begin making large numbers of calls, companies may need new ways to identify those calls and determine how they should be handled.

There is also the question of transparency. Users need to understand what an AI agent is doing, what information it has access to and when it requires approval before completing an important action.

The AI race is becoming more hands on

The competition between companies such as Google and Meta is increasingly moving beyond who can build the most capable chatbot.

The next stage centers on what those systems can actually accomplish.

Muse is designed to work across a person’s digital services and complete tasks in the background, while Google’s Gemini is gaining the ability to interact with businesses through phone calls.

That shift could eventually change how people interact with search engines, business websites and customer service departments.

For now, Google’s calling capability remains an experiment available to a limited group of users. But the direction is clear: AI assistants are increasingly being designed not just to tell people what to do, but to do more of the work themselves.

data.title: Google and OpenAI join AI safety push
data.description:
Google, OpenAI and Anthropic are moving closer to creating a shared organization focused on artificial intelligence safety standards, potentially giving the industry a common framework for evaluating some of its most advanced systems.


The proposed group, tentatively called the Standards Authority for Frontier AI, or SAFA, would be developed by the companies themselves rather than operating as a government regulator. Current reporting indicates that the organization could launch toward the end of 2026 or in early 2027.


The effort comes as policymakers, technology companies and researchers continue debating how increasingly capable AI systems should be tested and monitored. Discussions among the three companies have reportedly been underway for months, following a proposal from Google DeepMind chief Demis Hassabis for an AI standards organization modeled in part on the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority.

What the proposed AI group could do

SAFA is expected to focus on establishing common practices for evaluating advanced AI models before they are released.

Among the ideas under discussion are independent testing, standards for reporting safety and security incidents and requirements or qualifications for third-party organizations that audit AI models and laboratories.

The goal would be to create standards that could be applied across companies rather than having each AI developer establish completely separate approaches to testing and reporting.

The proposal remains in development, however. No formal organization has been launched, and details such as its final structure, leadership and authority have not been settled.

The initiative would also be voluntary rather than a replacement for government regulation. Without federal authority, the organization would not automatically have the same enforcement powers as a government agency.

Government involvement has been part of the discussion

The current industry-led approach follows an earlier proposal for greater government involvement.

Hassabis’ July proposal envisioned a U.S.-led standards body that would bring together government officials, industry participants and independent technical experts. The concept was compared with FINRA, which oversees the U.S. securities industry.

The companies subsequently began discussing how they could establish safety standards even without a government-backed organization. OpenAI confirmed in September that it had been working with Google and Anthropic on AI safety issues.

That shift is significant because the proposed SAFA would be created by the companies developing frontier AI systems rather than by lawmakers or federal regulators.

AI companies face growing pressure over safety

The discussions come as AI developers face increasing attention over how advanced models are tested before and after release.

Anthropic has recently emphasized outside evaluations as part of its approach to developing increasingly capable systems. Its latest Claude Opus 5.5 release included testing by external organizations, including METR and Frontier Design.

OpenAI has also called for stronger safety practices. In a September policy discussion, the company outlined proposals involving alignment research and the challenges associated with increasingly capable AI systems.

The broader industry debate includes questions about whether companies should rely primarily on voluntary commitments or whether governments should establish binding requirements.

OpenAI has separately advocated for national AI safety requirements, including independent assessments, cybersecurity measures and incident reporting for advanced systems.

The proposed framework faces questions

An industry led standards organization could provide a common system for evaluating AI models, but its eventual influence would depend on who participates and how its standards are applied.

The three companies involved are among the major developers of frontier AI systems, but they do not represent the entire industry. Other technology companies would have to decide whether to participate or adopt the proposed standards.

Questions about independence could also become important. If companies help create the rules used to evaluate their own technology, outside testing and transparent reporting could play a significant role in determining how credible the system becomes.

For now, SAFA remains a proposal rather than an operating organization. The companies are still working through its structure and leadership, with a possible launch expected by late 2026 or early 2027.

If established, the organization could become one part of a broader effort to create consistent safety practices as AI systems continue to become more capable.

data.title: Claude down? Here’s what we know about the outage
data.description:
Anthropic is investigating elevated error rates affecting Claude, Claude Cowork and Claude Code as users report trouble accessing the AI service.

If Claude suddenly stopped working on Tuesday, Sept. 29, you were not necessarily alone. Users attempting to access Anthropic’s popular AI assistant across the web, mobile apps and desktop appeared to be running into authentication and processing problems, leaving some unable to use the service.


The disruption quickly drew attention as reports of problems began climbing. For people who rely on Claude for writing, coding, research and everyday tasks, the outage was a reminder of how quickly a cloud-based AI service can become inaccessible when something goes wrong behind the scenes.


Anthropic has acknowledged that it is investigating elevated error rates affecting several of its services.

Claude users hit unexpected errors

Reports indicated that the problems were not limited to one platform. Users attempting to connect through Claude’s website, iOS and Android apps, as well as the desktop experience, encountered errors while trying to start or continue conversations.

Some users were met with messages indicating that their requests could not be processed. Others appeared to have trouble authenticating their accounts, making it difficult to get into Claude in the first place.

The issue also appeared to affect users with paid subscriptions. That matters because it has become more than a casual chatbot for many customers. Its paid tiers are used by professionals, developers and other users who depend on consistent access to AI tools.

Third-party outage tracking also began showing a noticeable increase in reports, suggesting the problem was broader than isolated account or device issues.

What Anthropic says about the outage

Anthropic’s status page confirmed that the company was investigating elevated error rates across Claude and related products.

The reported disruption included Claude itself, Claude Cowork and Claude Code, indicating that the problem was potentially affecting several parts of Anthropic’s broader AI ecosystem rather than a single interface.

At this stage, the company had not publicly identified a specific root cause or provided a definitive timeline for a full resolution.

That leaves users with an important distinction: an outage can be confirmed without its underlying cause being immediately known. Until Anthropic completes its investigation, it remains unclear whether the disruption stems from infrastructure, authentication, software or another technical issue.

Why the Claude disruption matters

Claude has become a significant player in the rapidly expanding AI assistant market, competing for users who increasingly incorporate generative AI into work and personal routines.

When a service like Claude experiences an outage, the consequences can extend beyond someone being unable to ask a chatbot a question. Developers may lose access to coding tools, workers may be unable to retrieve information from ongoing conversations, and businesses using AI-powered workflows can face interruptions.

For individual users, the experience can be especially frustrating when the service appears to work on one device but fails on another. Authentication errors can also make it difficult to determine whether the problem is with an account or with the platform itself.

What its users can do now

If it is not working, users can check Anthropic’s official status page for updates rather than repeatedly attempting to sign in or reinstall the app.

It may also help to:

  • Check whether the outage is affecting multiple Claude services.
  • Try again later if Anthropic is reporting an active incident.
  • Avoid repeatedly changing account settings while the company investigates.
  • Save important work locally when possible to reduce disruption during future outages.

For now, the most significant development is that Anthropic has acknowledged the service problems and is investigating them. Until the company provides more information, users may have to wait for the affected services to stabilize.

The outage also highlights a growing reality of the AI era: as these tools become woven into everyday work, even a temporary service interruption can quickly become a much bigger inconvenience.

Source: techradar

data.title: Apple’s iOS 27.0.1 update brings 3 essential iPhone fixes
data.description:
iPhone users, it’s time to check your settings.


Apple has released iOS 27.0.1, the first minor update since iOS 27 arrived earlier this month. The new software, which carries the build number 24A446, doesn’t bring any flashy new features. Instead, it focuses on fixing a handful of frustrating bugs that some users have run into since upgrading.


The update is available for every iPhone that supports iOS 27. However, two of its three main fixes are aimed specifically at the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max, Apple’s newest and most advanced models.

Here’s a closer look at the three fixes included in the release.

1. Face ID restart fix

The most notable fix addresses a problem with Face ID on the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max. Some owners found that their phones could unexpectedly restart when Face ID failed to recognize them.

Affected users also reported that their devices would sometimes freeze or have trouble when using Face ID inside apps. Because so many people rely on Face ID to unlock their phones, sign in to accounts and approve payments, this bug could be especially disruptive during everyday use.

2. Camera color artifact fix

The second fix involves the camera on a small number of iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max devices. In certain lighting conditions, photos taken at 2x zoom with an aperture of f/1.48 could show an unwanted color artifact.

While the issue only affected a limited number of phones, it’s the kind of glitch that can be especially annoying for anyone who bought a Pro model for its camera. The update should help ensure those shots come out looking the way they’re supposed to.

3. Touchscreen responsiveness fix

The third fix has a broader reach. Apple corrected a bug that could cause the touchscreen to stop responding if a user opened Notification Center and Control Center at the same time.

Unlike the first two fixes, this issue wasn’t limited to the newest Pro models. It could affect iPhones running iOS 27 more generally, making this update worth installing even if you don’t own an iPhone 18 Pro.

Updates for other Apple devices

The iPhone isn’t the only device getting attention. Apple also released iPadOS 27.0.1 for iPad and visionOS 27.0.1 for Apple Vision Pro alongside the new iPhone software.

Owners of older devices that can’t run the latest software haven’t been left out either. Apple has also made iOS 26.7.1 and iPadOS 26.7.1 available for those models.

How to install iOS 27.0.1

Getting the update only takes a few taps. Open the Settings app on your iPhone, tap General and then select Software Update. Once iOS 27.0.1 appears, tap Update Now or Download and Install, and enter your passcode if you’re asked for it. Keep your phone connected to power and Wi-Fi while the update installs, since the process can take several minutes and your iPhone will restart when it’s finished.

If you’d rather not check for updates yourself, you can turn on Automatic Updates from the same Software Update screen. With that setting on, your iPhone will download and install new versions of iOS on its own, usually overnight while it’s charging.

Before you update

It’s always a smart idea to back up your iPhone before installing any software update. A backup through iCloud or your computer can protect your photos, messages and other important data in the rare event that something goes wrong during the installation.

It’s also a good idea to make sure your phone has enough free storage space for the download. If your iPhone is nearly full, clearing out old apps, videos or files ahead of time can help the update go smoothly.

For anyone who has been dealing with Face ID restarts, camera glitches or an unresponsive screen, iOS 27.0.1 should bring welcome relief.

Source: The Mac Observer

data.title: Claude Sonnet 5.5 is here. Can rivals match 30% faster?
data.description:
Anthropic has released Claude Sonnet 5.5, an update to its mid-tier AI model that the company says works faster and costs less to run per task, even though its per-token price stays unchanged from its predecessor.


Speed and cost gains without a price change

Anthropic says Sonnet 5.5 generates output more than 30% faster than Sonnet 5 and can cut the total cost of completing a task by as much as 30%. That savings comes primarily from the model using fewer tokens and fewer tool calls to reach a result, rather than from any reduction in the underlying API price.


Sonnet 5.5 keeps the same rate as Sonnet 5, at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, with a discount to $0.20 per million tokens on cached input and $2.50 per million tokens on cache writes. Opus 5.5, Anthropic’s flagship model released the week prior, costs $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output tokens.

Closing the gap with Opus

Anthropic’s own evaluation results suggest Sonnet 5.5 now performs close to Opus 5.5 on several benchmarks. On GDPval-AA, which measures performance on tasks drawn from real-world occupations, Sonnet 5.5 scored 1844, nearly matching Opus 5.5’s 1846 and well ahead of Sonnet 5’s 1449. On AA-Briefcase, Sonnet 5.5 reached 1811 against Opus 5.5’s 1822. The model scored 80.1% on OSWorld 2.1, a partial computer-use evaluation, compared with 81.8% for Opus 5.5 and just 57% for Sonnet 5.

Coding performance stood out in particular. On Terminal-Bench 4.0, an agentic coding benchmark, Sonnet 5.5 scored 70.6%, ahead of Opus 5.5’s 66.4% and far above Sonnet 5’s 10.3%. On CursorBench 4.0, it reached 55.5%, narrowly behind Opus 5.5’s 57.8%.

Anthropic maintains that Opus 5.5 remains the stronger choice for ambiguous, open-ended work requiring sustained judgment, while positioning Sonnet 5.5 for more defined tasks like debugging, document creation and interface design. On some evaluations, the company says Sonnet 5.5 running at low or medium effort can beat Sonnet 5’s best score at roughly a tenth of the cost per task.

What early enterprise testing found

Several companies that tested Sonnet 5.5 ahead of launch reported efficiency gains beyond the benchmark scores. Box’s VP of AI Products said the model caught errors its predecessor missed while running 2.4 times faster and using 12% fewer total tokens.

Zendesk found tickets processed 20% faster with fewer incorrect decisions across hundreds of support cases. Slack’s testing showed the model outperforming Sonnet 5 on nearly all of its offline evaluations while needing fewer steps and about 14% fewer output tokens, with no prompt changes required.

Coding platform Lovable reported roughly a third fewer tool calls and about half as many shell executions to complete coding jobs, while Base44 found that across 118 real application builds, Sonnet 5.5 matched Opus 5’s results in an average of 3.6 iterations, compared with 7.7 for Opus 5, while producing the fewest failed tool calls among the models it tested.

A crowded field of mid-tier models

Sonnet 5.5 enters a market where competitors are pricing similarly capable models aggressively. OpenAI’s GPT-6 Sol, released the prior week, matches Sonnet 5.5’s rate of $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, with a larger 1.05 million token context window.

Google is pricing more aggressively with Gemini 3.8 Flash, offered at an introductory $0.75 per million input tokens and $3.75 per million output tokens through the end of 2026, before standard pricing rises to $1.50 and $7.50 respectively starting Jan. 1, 2027.

Chinese AI lab Xiaomi has taken a different approach entirely, releasing its MiMo-V2.6-Pro and Flash models under a permissive MIT license that allows free download and customization, while still pricing them affordably over the API for those who prefer hosted access.

New safeguards accompany the release

Sonnet 5.5 is the first Sonnet model to ship with cybersecurity safeguards modeled on those used in Anthropic’s highest-capability systems. Routine software development and vulnerability remediation work normally, but the company says some higher-risk cybersecurity requests will automatically route to Sonnet 5 instead.

Anthropic also introduced new protections against what it calls model distillation attacks, in which outside parties attempt to replicate a model’s capabilities by querying it at scale, along with classifiers designed to block extraction of the model’s internal reasoning.

Some critics have questioned that framing, noting that many AI labs, including Anthropic, have trained their own models on large amounts of data gathered from outside sources without direct compensation or consent from the original creators. Biology-related safeguards remain unchanged from Sonnet 5.

Availability and what comes next

Sonnet 5.5 is available through Anthropic directly, as well as Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud and Microsoft Azure, with support for zero data retention. Developers can access it through the Claude Platform using the model identifier claude-sonnet-5-5.

Anthropic says an updated Claude Haiku 5.5, aimed at high-volume, cost-sensitive workloads, will follow in the coming weeks, though no specific release date has been announced.

data.title: Should Sony worry as PS5 emulation gains alarming speed?
data.description:
Marvel’s Wolverine has been on store shelves for less than two weeks. Its main menu is already loading on a PC.


A short clip posted to X on Sept. 28 by user Jose Coixao shows KytyPS5, an open-source PlayStation 5 emulator, booting the newest PS5 exclusive to its menu. The catch is a big one. The menu reportedly crawls at about 2 frames per second, and the video shows no gameplay. Still, for a game that launched on Sept. 15, the milestone shows how quickly PS5 emulation is moving.


What the Wolverine clip actually shows

The demo ran on a machine far beyond a typical gaming setup, pairing an Nvidia GeForce RTX 5090 graphics card with an AMD Ryzen 7 7800X3D processor. Even with that hardware, the menu moved in slow motion.

Two open questions remain. The clip does not show Wolverine going in-game, and it’s unclear whether Coixao used the standard version of KytyPS5 or a modified build that isn’t publicly available. Reaching a menu is an early step, and finishing a game is a much longer road.

AnyPS5 is working on a project that could allow PS5 games to run natively on Windows and Linux, without emulation.

They want to convert PS5 game executables so they can run directly on PC hardware but the project is still in its early stages.

According to the developer, AnyPS5… pic.twitter.com/d0LsqVO7IX

— Pirat_Nation 🔴 (@Pirat_Nation) September 24, 2026

How fast KytyPS5 has improved

The emulator’s progress over the past few months helps explain why this clip got attention. Based on reporting from TweakTown and Android Authority, the path looks like this:

  1. In July, KytyPS5 had just reached the menus of Grand Theft Auto V and ran Quake II at about 7 FPS with visual glitches.
  2. About a month later, footage showed GTA V playing through its North Yankton prologue.
  3. Demon’s Souls then climbed from 1 to 2 FPS to between 10 and 18 FPS.
  4. New footage from YouTube channel PSXTech shows Demon’s Souls hitting 40 to 50 FPS on an Intel Core i9-14900K and an RTX 5090, reportedly using a closed or modified benchmark build.
  5. Now Wolverine, less than two weeks after release, has reached its main menu.

The Demon’s Souls jump stands out most. The game only began running in-game less than a month ago.

Which PS5 games already run in-game

Android Authority reports that KytyPS5 currently goes in-game in a range of titles, including Astro’s Playroom, Crash Bandicoot 4, Hitman: World of Assassination, Uncharted 4, Spider-Man: Miles Morales, Silent Hill f and Tekken 8.

Silent Hill 2 Remake is a case where reports differ. TweakTown says the main KytyPS5 build still crashes on it. A developer did get the remake running in-game using KytyPlus, a fork of the emulator, on a PC with an integrated Radeon 840M graphics chip, a far more modest setup than the RTX 5090 rigs behind most of these demos.

The Wolverine milestone comes with caveats

The most impressive results so far have come from modified or unreleased builds. That makes it hard to know what an average user can reproduce with the public version on GitHub.

Hardware is the other barrier. An RTX 5090 is a top-tier graphics card, and even it could manage only a slow-moving Wolverine menu. Android Authority also cautioned that running PlayStation 5games on Android phones is likely at least four or five years away.

What comes next for PS5 emulation

The PlayStation 5 is still Sony’s current console, alongside the PS5 Pro, which makes this pace of progress unusual. Emulation usually catches up to a system years after its peak, not while its newest exclusives are still arriving.

For now, Wolverine on PC is a proof of concept, not a playable game. If the improvements seen in Demon’s Souls and GTA V carry over, though, the gap between a 2 FPS menu and real gameplay could close faster than many expect.

data.title: Everything revealed at Minecraft Live 2026
data.description:
Minecraft is getting its biggest structural addition in over a decade. At this year’s Minecraft Live showcase, Mojang confirmed a new dimension called The Sift, the game’s first entirely new reality since The End arrived back in 2011, alongside a run of other updates spanning a new spin-off game, fresh biomes and a long awaited console release.

The Sift joins Minecraft’s core dimensions

The Sift will debut first inside Minecraft Dungeons II, the upcoming spin-off launching Sept. 29, before arriving in the main game’s Java and Bedrock editions sometime in 2027. Once it lands in vanilla Minecraft, it will become the game’s fourth official dimension alongside the Overworld, the Nether and the End.


Mojang shared relatively few mechanical details about how The Sift will function in the base game, offering mostly a visual glimpse during the stream along with a look at one of its new mobs. Within Minecraft Dungeons II, the studio describes the realm as vibrant and filled with souls, featuring distinct areas known as the Meadow and the Carapace. One of its new residents already generating buzz among fans is a small blue rabbit spotted in early footage.

Minecraft Dungeons II expands on the original

Dungeons II builds on the foundation of the original Minecraft Dungeons, an isometric co-op hack and slash spin-off that stood out for successfully translating Minecraft’s charm into a very different genre. The sequel centers on the hub town of Bravehaven, where players investigate a spreading soul corruption across interconnected overworld levels themed around the Deep Dark and Ancient Cities, including an appearance from the Warden.

The gameplay itself gets several meaningful additions, including the long requested ability to jump, along with new aerial attacks. Armor now splits into the series’ traditional four piece sets alongside new talismans that provide passive bonuses. Levels are also larger and more interconnected than in the original, giving players more freedom to choose their own path rather than selecting missions from a linear map.

New biomes and creative tools for the main game

Vanilla is also getting underground ice caves, a rare cold biome variant packed with ore deposits and easy access to ice. The caves introduce a new frozen zombie enemy that throws ice projectiles and can freeze players who get caught in repeated melee exchanges, though players can just as easily throw the ice back at enemies or each other.

The ice crystals scattered throughout the caves double as a decorative item and an emergency light source, and can also be used to craft freezing potions. Experienced players will likely start experimenting with turning regular zombies into frozen ones by exposing them to powdered snow.

On the creative side, Mojang Chief Creative Officer Jens Bergenström discussed changes aimed at making player created content easier to build and access for both newcomers and professional creators.

Today at Minecraft LIVE: Dungeons II, our first new dimension in more than 14 years, new ways for creators to build, Minecraft on Nintendo Switch 2, and more.

More than 300,000 people play Minecraft for the first time on an average day. After 17+ years and 425M+ copies sold, I… pic.twitter.com/fdhkwuh258

— ASHA (@asha_shar) September 26, 2026

A new set of sound effect packs is also coming to the Marketplace later this year, allowing players to customize how the base game or their own creations sound, though pricing and an exact release date have not been announced. Bergenström also clarified that Mojang does not plan to release a content update specifically for the End dimension, choosing instead to prioritize these creator focused tools.

Switch 2 launch and other announcements

Minecraft is officially coming to Nintendo Switch 2 on Oct. 27, bringing updated visuals closer to the versions currently available on Xbox and PlayStation 5. Mojang also touched on a Minecraft themed section opening at Chessington World of Adventures in the UK, along with a companion themed hotel, both aimed primarily at UK based fans.

With The Sift now confirmed for both the upcoming spin-off and the core game, and considering how significantly past dimension additions like the Nether and the End reshaped how Minecraft is played, its eventual full release next year is likely to mark one of the more significant shifts in the game’s recent history.
